title: nEmesis-guided inspections find 64% more C-or-worse venues than standard inspections in Las Vegas
summary: SNHD double-blind trial from 2 January 2015: Twitter-mined nEmesis flags yielded 9 vs 6 demerits per inspection and 11 vs 7 venues graded C or worse (64% more).
account: The Southern Nevada Health District (SNHD) began a controlled experiment with nEmesis, a University of Rochester system that applies a support-vector-machine language model to geotagged tweets to rank Las Vegas food venues by foodborne-illness risk, on 2 January 2015. During the first three months environmental health specialists inspected 142 venues, half chosen by nEmesis and half under the standard protocol, with inspectors blind to which was which. Adaptive inspections uncovered 9 demerits per inspection versus 6 (p = 0.019) and found 11 venues graded C or worse versus 7 for the control arm, a 64% improvement; the abstract summarizes this as 63% more effective. Side findings included an unpermitted seafood establishment and a food handler working with an influenza-like illness. The authors estimate, from CDC outbreak averages, that adaptive inspections saved 71 infections and 4.4 hospitalizations over the three months and could prevent over 9,126 cases and 557 hospitalizations a year if all of Las Vegas's 35,000+ annual inspections were adaptive; SNHD performed 5 foodborne-illness investigations between 2 January and 31 March 2015 against 11 in the same window the year before. The date given is the end of that reported window.
purpose: Rank Las Vegas food venues by predicted foodborne-illness risk, inferred from Twitter posts, so that health inspectors can prioritize the riskiest venues.
system: nEmesis (SVM language model over geotagged tweets with a web interface for inspectors)
developer: University of Rochester (Adam Sadilek, Henry Kautz and colleagues)
taxonomy_note: Classed as benefit created on the observed inspection yield (demerits and serious-grade venues found in a controlled, double-blind comparison). The illness and hospitalization savings are model-based estimates, so the societal depth is left null. Peer-reviewed (AAAI/IAAI deployed-application paper) with the deployer's staff as co-authors.

ratings.reason: In 142 blinded inspections the nEmesis arm uncovered 9 vs 6 demerits per inspection (p = 0.019) and 11 vs 7 venues graded C or worse, plus an unpermitted seafood establishment and a sick food handler.

The 71 infections and 4.4 hospitalizations said to be saved are estimates from CDC outbreak averages; the drop in foodborne-illness investigations (5 vs 11) is an uncontrolled year-on-year comparison, not a measured outcome.

ai_role.statement: The AI chose which venues to inspect; because the comparison was a controlled double-blind design with 142 venues split between nEmesis and standard protocol, the difference in findings is attributable to the AI's venue selection. The developers (Rochester) are distinct from the deployer (SNHD), though SNHD staff co-authored the paper, which was peer-reviewed as an IAAI deployed paper.

evidence.citation: Sadilek A, Kautz H, DiPrete L, Labus B, Portman E, Teitel J, Silenzio V. Deploying nEmesis: Preventing Foodborne Illness by Data Mining Social Media. Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence 30(2):3982-3989 (2016). doi:10.1609/aaai.v30i2.19072
evidence.title: Deploying nEmesis: Preventing Foodborne Illness by Data Mining Social Media
evidence.quote: We determined that adaptive inspections uncover significantly more demerits: 9 vs. 6 per inspection (p-value of 0.019).

produced_by: Dense geotagged social-media posting across a metropolitan area
A health department willing to assign half of a matched inspection sample to algorithm-flagged venues
A graded inspection protocol (demerits, letter grades) that makes arms comparable
must_hold: Access to geotagged public posts and venue locations as available through the Twitter and Google Places APIs in 2015
Inspectors blinded to the source of the assignment
Enough flagged venues per day to schedule adaptive inspections

echoes.setting: Las Vegas (May-August 2016) and Chicago (November 2016-March 2017), Google's FINDER using aggregated web search and location data
echoes.model_version: FINDER (successor model by the same lead author, not nEmesis)
echoes.source: Sadilek et al. 2018, npj Digital Medicine, doi:10.1038/s41746-018-0045-1

headline: nEmesis-guided inspections find 64% more C-or-worse venues
metric: found 11 venues graded C or worse versus 7 for the control arm, a 64% improvement

revisions.change: Record drafted from the cited sources.

claim_basis: The makers' peer-reviewed study is on file. There is no independent source and no finding by a regulator or court.
